# The Country of Night

On January 17, 1994, at 4:31 in the morning, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck Northridge, California, tearing apart freeways and apartment blocks and, in the chaos, knocking out electrical power across much of Los Angeles. In the hours that followed, residents who wandered outside their homes saw an enormous, unfamiliar silvery cloud arched over the city — so strange that some called emergency services, and the Griffith Observatory reportedly fielded anxious calls asking what the thing in the sky could be. The answer was embarrassing and wonderful at once. It was the Milky Way: our own galaxy, the collected light of hundreds of billions of suns, hidden for generations behind the city's glow and revealed for a single night by disaster. Plenty of Angelenos had simply never seen it.

I keep thinking about that silvery cloud — about what it means that a whole civilization could lose track of the galaxy it lives inside, and about the larger territory it stands for. Darkness used to be a place where people lived. Over the past two centuries we have done to the night what we did to the wilderness: surveyed it, annexed it, lit it, and largely forgotten it. This is an essay about that forgotten country — what it was, why we left it, what the leaving cost, and whether any of it can be gotten back.

## I. Another Country

For nearly all of human history, night was not the day with the lights turned off. It was a different jurisdiction with different laws. When the sun went down, the world reorganized itself around fire: doors barred, travel suspended, law thinned to whatever the neighbors could enforce by earshot. The old vocabulary still carries the residue. We call bad dreams *nightmares*, and the *mare* in question was once taken literally — a demon that settled on sleepers' chests in the dark. Night was populated: by ghosts, saints, witches, the restless dead, by dreams that people believed carried messages worth decoding.

Sleep itself had a different architecture. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, letters, court records, and medical manuals going back centuries, discovered that before the Industrial Revolution, Westerners typically did not sleep in one block. They slept twice. A "first sleep" began an hour or two after dusk. Around midnight people rose naturally into an interval of quiet wakefulness — contemporaries called it the watch — and prayed, tended the fire, talked with family or neighbors, reviewed their dreams, made love (some physicians recommended the interval as the best time to conceive a child), or simply lay listening to the house settle. Then came the "second sleep," which ran until dawn. Ekirch found hundreds of references to this pattern across languages and eras, from Chaucer to nineteenth-century memoirs. It wasn't insomnia. It was the default shape of human rest.

Modern experiments quietly confirm him. When researchers in the 1990s mimicked preindustrial winter conditions — fourteen hours of darkness per night, sustained for weeks — subjects' sleep split neatly into two segments with a calm, unhurried interval between them. What we now diagnose as middle-of-the-night insomnia may partly be an artifact: the ghost of the watch, surfacing in bodies that expect a long dark and receive eight hours between alarms.

Night was also, sensorially, richer than ours. Deprived of sight, the other senses expanded to fill the vacancy. Hearing mapped the neighborhood: watchmen crying the hours, dogs answering one another across fields, wind working the eaves, the particular creak of a house cooling after sunset. Smell sharpened — woodsmoke, tallow, rain arriving on distant dust. Touch governed the last steps to the privy and back. Darkness slowed everything down. It was thick, textured, and full of information, not merely the absence of a switch.

## II. The Price of a Flame

Why did our ancestors accept all this darkness? Not because they were stoic, and not because they loved it. Because light was ruinously expensive. The economist William Nordhaus spent part of his career reconstructing the price of illumination across five millennia, converting everything — sesame-oil lamps, tallow, kerosene, kilowatt-hours — into a single currency: how much labor does an hour of light cost? His rough answers are staggering. In ancient Babylon, an hour of decent lamplight cost on the order of a day's wages, by some reconstructions considerably more. Even in 1800, a candle still demanded hours of work for every hour of light it gave. Today the same illumination costs a fraction of a second of median pay. The decline is so steep that no ordinary chart can hold it.

The consequences followed directly. Poor households did not light their evenings because they could not afford to. The British poor made do with rushlights — rush stems stripped and dried, dipped in kitchen grease, producing a smoky flame that lasted perhaps a quarter hour and filled the room with the stink of burning fat. Better-off families burned tallow candles, which guttered and wept; beeswax was for churches and the rich; spermaceti from whales burned cleaner and costlier still; kerosene arrived after 1859 and democratized a decent flame. "Up with the sun, down with the sun" was not an agricultural romance. It was a budget line. Everyone knew darkness intimately because everyone returned to it nightly, the way we now return to sleep.

## III. Annexation

Then, within a few generations, night fell. First came gas: demonstrated on London's Pall Mall in 1807, piped beneath Baltimore by 1817, and soon threaded through every major capital. Streetlights changed the physics of the city. A metropolis that had contracted at dusk now kept going; commerce, policing, and promenading extended themselves into hours that had belonged to thieves, lovers, and insomniacs. Paris earned its nickname, the City of Light. Then electricity finished the job: Edison's practical bulb in 1879, the Pearl Street station powering Lower Manhattan in 1882, arc lamps blazing along the great boulevards like captured lightning. Night was formally annexed. Shift work invented a workforce that slept while the sun stood watch. Diners, cinemas, neon, night baseball. "The city that never sleeps" is a boast that would have been gibberish in 1720; every city slept, because the alternative cost too much.

Our own era completed the process by making light effectively free. The LED delivered lumens for pennies, and we responded the way economies respond to anything cheap: we stopped counting. Roads, billboards, vacant office floors, parking lots at three in the morning lit like operating theaters for absolutely no one. The night is now, over most of the inhabited world, a dim photocopy of the day. Nobody decided this. It is simply what happens when a boundary disappears and no one remembers there was ever a border.

## IV. What the Floodlights Took

Start with the obvious casualty. According to the 2016 World Atlas of Artificial Night Sky Brightness, more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. About a third of our species — including sixty percent of Europeans and eighty percent of North Americans — can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. And the loss compounds quickly: recent measurements suggest the glow is brightening by nearly ten percent a year. Each generation resets its baseline. Children now grow up believing the night contains four stars, because four stars is what the night contains where they live.

But skyglow is only the headline. Living things evolved under a strict alternation of light and dark, and that alternation was information — a clock, a compass, a calendar — running for hundreds of millions of years before anyone built a lamp. We are now broadcasting static over the channel. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the sand and instinctively scrabble toward the brighter horizon, which for sixty million years meant moonlight on moving water. Beachfront development reverses the cue: the condominiums outshine the surf, and thousands of baby turtles crawl inland to die on the highway. Songbirds migrate overwhelmingly at night, navigating by stars and magnetic fields; city lights draw them in like snares, and collisions with illuminated glass kill on the order of hundreds of millions of birds a year in the United States alone. Hence the "Lights Out" campaigns that dim skyscrapers during migration season — a modest, partial truce.

Even the moth at the porch light, that stock image of stupidity, turns out to be a tragedy of confusion rather than desire. High-speed camera studies published in 2024 show that insects don't steer toward lamps because they love them; they tilt their backs toward the brightest point in view, an ancient reflex that assumes the brightest thing around is the open sky. Trap a moth beneath a bulb and "up" points everywhere and nowhere; it circles until it drops. Multiply that porch light by a billion porches and you begin to grasp the scale. Add the fireflies whose luminous courtship is drowned in ambient glare, the corals whose synchronized spawning — timed for ages to the moon — falls out of rhythm under experimental skyglow, the trees that bud earlier and hold their leaves later under streetlamps, and the humans whose evening screens suppress melatonin and shove their circadian clocks sideways. Almost nothing alive is immune. We are not exempt; we are just the only species doing this to ourselves on purpose.

## V. The Inner Night

All of this is measurable, which makes it discussable in polite company. But the deepest losses are the ones without units. Consider what the night sky was: the first shared artwork of the species, the oldest archive we possess. Long before writing, every culture looked up and saw its stories pinned there — hunters and bears, rivers and queens, the scattered campfires of the ancestors. The stars were simultaneously a calendar (when Sirius rises, the Nile floods), a chart (find the Pole Star and cross the featureless Pacific), a scripture, and a clock. To lose the stars is not merely to lose a pretty view. It is to inherit a museum and never be able to visit.

Darkness also performed quieter, inward work. With nothing left to look at, the mind turned around and faced itself. Night was when stories were told, songs worked out, grief metabolized, schemes dreamed past the point of plausibility. There is a reason so much scripture and so much poetry happens at night. We have replaced those unfilled hours with the most efficient gap-filler ever devised — the glowing screen, a pocket sun that serves us daylight at midnight and holds our faces in its little pool of light. We haven't only abolished the outer dark. We've abolished the inner one, the necessary dark, and then wonder why the mind, denied its nightly fallow field, lies twitching at two in the morning, scrolling through the equivalent of noon.

And darkness, properly entered, is not an absence at all. It is a sense that must be switched on. Give your eyes twenty minutes away from light and the world rematerializes: color drains out, but form blooms; distances clarify; you discover you see best slightly off-center — because in the dark the tightly packed cones of your central gaze go blind and the rod-rich periphery takes over, which is why experienced stargazers look *beside* faint objects rather than at them. Under a genuinely dark sky, your bare eye reaches the Andromeda Galaxy, two and a half million light-years away: the most distant thing most human beings will ever see without optics, its photons setting out long before Homo sapiens existed. Wait longer, in darker places, and stranger things surface — the pale cone of zodiacal light, the sky's own faint airglow, the mysterious counter-glow called the Gegenschein. None of this requires equipment. It requires only the one condition we have systematically destroyed: enough darkness, held long enough, for your own eyes to come fully awake.

## VI. Taking It Back

Here is the good news, and it is genuinely good: light pollution is the easiest environmental catastrophe to reverse. Acid rain requires scrubbing a century of chemistry out of the water cycle. Carbon requires rebuilding civilization's energy spine. Excess light requires, essentially, aiming. Shield fixtures so they throw light down rather than up. Choose warm spectra instead of blue-white. Dim after midnight, when the streets stand empty anyway. Switch off what serves no one. None of this is sacrifice on any meaningful scale. It is manners.

The movement already exists. Since 1988 the International Dark-Sky Association has certified sanctuaries where darkness is protected like habitat — Utah's Natural Bridges became the first dark-sky park in 2007; the island of Sark, Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand, and Wales' Bannau Brycheiniog followed. Cities from Chicago to New York dim their towers during bird migration; Florida beach towns tune their lighting around turtle season. These efforts remain small against the tide of new LEDs washing over the developing world, but they prove something essential: the border can be redrawn. The night can be rezoned.

And individually, the country is closer than you think. Drive forty minutes past the edge of the sprawl on a night near the new moon. Park, kill your headlights, and wait — really wait, twenty minutes, hands in pockets, letting your pupils drink. If you're fortunate enough to land under a Bortle-class-three sky or darker, you will see it: the river overhead, the thing the Angelenos mistook for weather. Most people who finally see it properly describe the same sequence of reactions — disbelief, then delight, then a peculiar vertigo, the feeling of having been shown a room in their own house they never knew existed.

## Coda

Somewhere ahead of us there will be another citywide blackout — storm, grid failure, something else entirely. And in that darkened city a person will step outside, look up, and see the Milky Way hanging there, enormous and improbable, and feel certain they are looking at a sign, an omen, a thing too vast to be merely astronomical. They will be right, though not in the way they think. # The Country of Night

Para 1: On January 17, 1994, at 4:31 in the morning, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck Northridge, California, tearing apart freeways and apartment blocks and, in the chaos, knocking out electrical power across much of Los Angeles. In the hours that followed, residents who wandered outside their homes reported seeing an enormous, unfamiliar silvery cloud arched over the city — so strange that some called emergency services, and the Griffith Observatory took anxious phone calls asking what the thing in the sky could be. The answer was embarrassing and wonderful at once. It was the Milky Way: our own galaxy, the collective light of hundreds of billions of suns, hidden for generations behind the city's glow and revealed for a single night by disaster. Plenty of Angelenos had simply never seen it.

Para 2: I've been thinking about that silvery cloud — about what it means that a whole civilization could lose track of the galaxy it lives inside, and about the larger territory it stands for. Darkness used to be a place where people lived. Over the past two centuries we have done to the night what we did to the wilderness: surveyed it, annexed it, lit it, and largely forgotten it. This is an essay about that forgotten country — what it was, why we left it, what the leaving cost, and whether any of it can be gotten back.

## I. Another Country

Para 3: For nearly all of human history, night was not the day with the lights turned off. It was a different jurisdiction with different laws. When the sun went down, the world reorganized itself around fire: doors barred, travel suspended, law thinned to whatever the neighbors could enforce by earshot. The old vocabulary still carries the residue. We call bad dreams nightmares, and the mare in question was once taken literally — a demon that settled on sleepers' chests in the dark. Night was populated: by ghosts, saints, witches, the dead, by dreams that people believed carried messages worth decoding.

Para 4: Sleep itself had a different architecture. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, letters, court records, and medical manuals going back centuries, discovered that before the Industrial Revolution, Westerners typically did not sleep in one block. They slept twice. A "first sleep" began an hour or two after dusk. Around midnight people rose naturally into an interval of quiet wakefulness — contemporaries called it the watch — and prayed, tended the fire, talked with family or neighbors, reviewed their dreams, made love (some physicians recommended the interval as the best time to conceive a child), or simply lay listening to the house breathe. Then came the "second sleep," which ran until dawn. Ekirch found hundreds of references to this pattern across languages and eras, from Chaucer to nineteenth-century diaries. It wasn't insomnia; it was the default shape of human rest.

Para 5: Modern experiments quietly confirm him. When researchers in the 1990s mimicked preindustrial winter conditions — fourteen hours of darkness per night, for weeks — subjects' sleep split neatly into two segments with a calm, distinctly non-anxious hour between them. What we call middle-of-the-night insomnia may partly be an artifact: the ghost of the watch, surfacing in bodies that expect a long dark and receive eight hours between alarms.

Para 6: Night was also, sensorially, richer than ours. Deprived of sight, the other senses expanded to fill it... hearing: watchmen calling hours, dogs, wind, the creak of a settling house; smell: woodsmoke, tallow, rain on dust. Darkness slowed everything down. It was thick.

## II. The Price of a Flame

Para 7: Why did our ancestors accept all this darkness? Not because they were stoic, and not because they loved it. Because light was ruinously expensive. The economist William Nordhaus spent part of his career reconstructing the price of illumination across five millennia, converting everything — sesame-oil lamps, candles, kerosene, kilowatts — into a single unit: how much labor does an hour of light cost? His rough answers are staggering. In ancient Babylon, an hour of decent lamplight cost something like a day's wages, by some reconstructions considerably more. Even in 1800, a tallow candle still demanded hours of work for every hour of light. Today the same illumination costs a fraction of a second of median pay. The drop is so steep that no ordinary chart can hold it.

Para 8: The consequences followed directly. Poor households did not light their evenings because they could not afford to. The British poor made do with rushlights — rush stems stripped of their skin, dried, and dipped in kitchen grease, producing a smoky flame that lasted perhaps a quarter hour and filled the room with the smell of burning fat. Better-off families burned tallow candles, which guttered and stank; beeswax was for churches and the rich; spermaceti from whales was cleaner and dearer still; kerosene arrived after 1859 and democratized a decent flame. "Up with the sun, down with the sun" was not an agricultural romance. It was a budget. Everyone knew darkness intimately because everyone returned to it nightly, the way we return to sleep.

## III. Annexation

Para 9: Then, within a few generations, night fell. First came gas: demonstrated on London's Pall Mall in 1807, piped through Baltimore by 1817, and soon threading beneath every major capital. Streetlights changed the physics of the city. A metropolis that had shrunk at dusk now kept going; commerce, policing, promenading extended themselves into hours that had belonged to thieves and insomniacs. Paris earned its nickname, the City of Light. Then electricity finished the job: Edison's practical bulb in 1879, the Pearl Street station powering Lower Manhattan in 1882, arc lamps blazing along the great boulevards like captured lightning. Night was formally annexed. Shift work invented a workforce that slept while the sun watched. Diners, cinemas, neon signs, night baseball. "The city that never sleeps" is a boast that would have been gibberish in 1720; every city slept, because the alternative cost too much.

Para 10: Our own era completed the process by making light effectively free. The LED delivered lumens for pennies, and we responded the way economies respond to anything cheap: we stopped counting. Roads, billboards, empty office floors, parking lots at three in the morning lit like operating theaters for absolutely no one. The night is now, over most of the inhabited world, a dim photocopy of the day. Nobody decided this. It is just what happens when a boundary disappears and no one remembers there was ever a border.

## IV. What the Floodlights Took

Para 11: Start with the obvious casualty. According to the 2016 World Atlas of Artificial Night Sky Brightness, more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. About a third of our species — including sixty percent of Europeans and eighty percent of North Americans — can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. And the loss compounds quickly: recent satellite measurements suggest the glow is brightening by nearly ten percent a year. Each generation resets its baseline. Children now grow up believing the night contains four stars, because four stars is what the night contains where they live.

Para 12: But skyglow is only the headline. Living things evolved under a strict alternation of light and dark, and that alternation was information — a clock, a compass, a calendar — running for hundreds of millions of years before anyone built a lamp. We are now broadcasting static over the channel. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the sand and instinctively scrabble toward the brighter horizon, which for sixty million years meant moonlight on waves. Beachfront development reverses the cue: the condos are brighter than the surf, and thousands of baby turtles crawl inland to die on the highway. Songbirds migrate overwhelmingly at night, navigating by stars and magnetic fields; city lights draw them in like snares, and collisions with illuminated glass kill on the order of hundreds of millions of birds a year in the United States alone. Hence the "Lights Out" campaigns that dim skyscrapers during migration seasons — a modest, partial truce.

Para 13: Even the humble moth at the porch light, that stock image of stupidity, turns out to be a tragedy of confusion rather than attraction. High-speed camera studies published in 2024 show that insects don't fly toward lamps because they love them; they tilt their backs toward the brightest point in view, an ancient reflex that assumes the brightest thing around is the open sky. Trap a moth under a bulb and "up" points everywhere and nowhere; it circles until it drops. Multiply that porch light by a billion porches and you begin to see the scale. Add the fireflies whose luminous courtship is drowned in ambient glare, the corals whose synchronized mass spawning — timed for millennia to the moon — desynchronizes under experimental skyglow, the trees that bud earlier and hold their leaves later under streetlamps, and the humans whose evening screens suppress melatonin and shove their circadian clocks sideways. Almost nothing alive is immune, ourselves included.

## V. The Inner Night

Para 14: All of this is measurable, which makes it discussable in polite company. But the deepest losses are the ones without units. Consider what the night sky was: the first shared artwork of the species, the oldest archive we have. Long before writing, every culture looked up and saw its stories pinned there — hunters and bears, rivers and queens, the scattered campfires of the ancestors. The stars were simultaneously a calendar (when Sirius rises, the Nile floods), a map (find the Pole Star, cross the featureless Pacific), a scripture, and a clock. To lose the stars is not merely to lose a pretty view. It is to lose access to the oldest gallery of human meaning — to inherit a museum and never be able to visit.

Para 15: Darkness also performed quieter, inward work. With nothing left to look at, the mind turned around and faced itself. Night was when stories were told, songs worked out, grief metabolized, plans dreamed past the point of plausibility. There is a reason so much scripture, so much poetry, happens at night. We have replaced those unfilled hours with the most efficient gap-filler ever devised — the glowing screen, a pocket sun that serves us daylight at midnight and holds our faces in its little pool of light. We haven't only abolished the outer dark. We've abolished the inner one, the necessary dark, and then wonder why the mind, denied its nightly fallow field, lies twitching at 2 a.m. scrolling through the equivalent of daylight.

Para 16: And darkness, properly entered, is not an absence at all. It is a sense that must be switched on. Give your eyes twenty minutes away from light and the world rematerializes: colors drain out, but forms bloom, distances clarify, and you discover you see best slightly off-center — because in the dark the densely packed cones of your central gaze go blind and the rod-rich periphery takes over, which is why experienced stargazers look beside faint objects rather than at them. Under a genuinely dark sky, your bare eye reaches the Andromeda Galaxy, two and a half million light years away: the most distant thing most human beings will ever see without optics, its light already en route before our genus existed. Wait longer, in darker places, and stranger things surface — the pale pyramid of zodiacal light, the sky's own faint airglow, the mysterious counter-glow called the Gegenschein. These are not exotic sights requiring equipment. They require only the one condition we have systematically destroyed: enough darkness, held long enough, for your own eyes to come fully awake.

## VI. Taking It Back

Para 17: Here is the good news, and it is genuinely good: light pollution is the easiest environmental catastrophe to reverse. Acid rain requires scrubbing a century of chemistry out of the water cycle. Carbon requires rebuilding civilization's energy spine. Excess light requires, essentially, aiming. Shield fixtures so they throw light down, not up. Choose warm spectra instead of blue-white. Dim after midnight, when the streets are empty anyway. Switch off what serves no one. None of this is sacrifice on any meaningful scale; it is manners.

Para 18: The movement already exists. Since 1988 the International Dark-Sky Association has certified sanctuaries where the dark is protected like habitat — Utah's Natural Bridges was the first dark-sky park, in 2007; the island of Sark, Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand, Wales' Bannau Brycheiniog followed. Cities from Chicago to New York dim their towers during bird migration; Florida beach towns manage their lighting around turtle season. These efforts remain tiny against the tide of new LEDs washing over the developing world, but they prove something essential: the border can be redrawn. The night can be rezoned.

Para 19: And individually, the country is closer than you think. Drive forty minutes past the edge of the sprawl, on a night near the new moon. Kill your headlights, let your eyes adapt, and wait. If you're lucky enough to find yourself under a Bortle-class-3 sky or darker, you will see it — the river overhead, the thing the Angelenos mistook for weather.

## Coda

Para 20: Somewhere ahead of us there will be another citywide blackout — storm, grid failure, war, who knows. And somewhere in that darkened city a person will step outside, look up, and see the Milky Way hanging there, enormous and improbable, and feel certain they are looking at a sign, an omen, a thing too vast to be merely astronomical. They will be right, though not in the way they think. It is merely astronomy, and it is also the accumulated light of a hundred billion suns, seen edge-on from inside, our own home rendered as a river of fog and fire.

Para 21: Darkness was never the absence of everything. It was the presence of everything too far away to see — patient, overhead, waiting all these years for our eyes to remember how.
